The pain is easing, but it's a nagging ache just the same. The rush-hour train bombings killed 191 people and wounded 1,800 others. It was March 11, 2004, during morning rush hour, that terrorists armed with powerful bombs boarded these same commuter train lines, unleashing an onslaught that killed 191 people and wounded 1,800 others. The attacks are the deadliest in Europe since the rise of al Qaeda. More than a year later on July 7, 2005, terrorists would stage bombings on the London transit system that killed 52 people and wounded hundreds more. The explosives were left on the Spanish trains in sports bags and backpacks -- sometimes placed under seats -- court documents say. The terrorists got off at various stations down the line, before cell-phone timers detonated 10 bombs in quick succession on four trains at three stations. Police dismantled another bomb that didn't explode. It provided vital clues that led to arrests. Eighteen people, mostly Islamic militants, have been convicted in the attacks. Watch more on the anniversary . Juan Carlos Garcia, an engineer who took the train later that same day, said he knows a couple whose daughter died in the attacks. "It was very tough, especially knowing it could have been you," Garcia said. "Now, you remember it, but not the same as when it just happened." Beata Sadecka, a regular commuter, says she rides cautiously. "Every day, when I get on the train, I always ride in the last car," Sadecka said. "I don't know why, for safety," she added, not quite sure of her motives. On one train, the first explosion was in a rear car and, as people ran forward to get away, they were hit by explosions in the middle cars, investigators have said. "People remember the March 11th attacks," said Vicente Jimenez, a deputy editor with El Pais newspaper, "and while conscious that the threat continues, you have to continue with your life." Memorial observations were scheduled throughout the day, including five minutes of silence for the victims. King Juan Carlos and Prime Minister Jose Luis Rodriguez Zapatero were not taking part in the public events. A victims group called their non-participation a slight. # Madrid remembers train bombing victims five years later

**MADRID, Spain (CNN) —** Spain paused Wednesday to remember the 191 people killed five years ago when bombs ripped through four crowded commuter trains in Madrid, carrying out the deadliest terrorist attack in the country’s history.

Relatives of the victims, survivors and government officials gathered at memorial sites across the capital, laying flowers and observing moments of silence for those killed in the March 11, 2004, attacks. More than 1,800 people were injured.

Ten bombs exploded within minutes during the morning rush hour aboard trains near Atocha station and at El Pozo and Santa Eugenia. Three other devices failed to detonate.

The attacks shocked Spain and came just three days before a national election. The government initially pointed to the Basque separatist group ETA, but investigators soon linked the bombings to Islamist extremists inspired by al Qaeda.

Public anger over the government’s handling of information about the investigation became a major election issue. The opposition Socialists won the vote, and incoming Prime Minister José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero later withdrew Spanish troops from Iraq.

In 2007, a Spanish court convicted 21 people on charges connected to the attacks, although several verdicts were later modified on appeal. Jamal Zougam, who was identified by witnesses as having been on one of the trains, was among those sentenced to thousands of years in prison under Spain’s system of calculating penalties for each victim. Spanish law limits the amount of time a prisoner may actually serve.

Seven leading suspects died in April 2004 when they detonated explosives in an apartment in the Madrid suburb of Leganés as police closed in. The blast also killed a police officer.

Five years later, the attacks remain known throughout Spain simply as **11-M**, shorthand for March 11. Memorials at Atocha station and other affected locations have become permanent reminders of the victims and of a morning that changed the country.

Wednesday’s commemorations were solemn and largely without political speeches, focusing instead on the dead, the injured and the families still living with the consequences.

Across Madrid, trains continued to arrive and depart as relatives placed candles and flowers beside plaques bearing the victims’ names.

## Madrid commuters carry on, five years after the 3/11 attacks

**MADRID, March 11, 2009** — Five years after bombs tore through Madrid’s morning commuter trains, the railway network is again packed at rush hour. For many passengers, returning to the same platforms and carriages has been an act of necessity—and, increasingly, routine—though announcements, abandoned bags and the approach of the anniversary can still revive memories of the attack.

On March 11, 2004, terrorists placed 13 backpack bombs on four packed Cercanías commuter trains traveling toward central Madrid. Ten devices exploded between about 7:37 and 7:40 a.m., striking trains at or near **Atocha, El Pozo and Santa Eugenia stations and on Calle Téllez**, close to Atocha. The other three devices failed to explode.

The bombings killed **191 people and wounded more than 1,800**, making them the deadliest terrorist attack in modern Spanish history. Investigators and the courts concluded that the attack was carried out by an Islamist extremist cell inspired by al-Qaeda. Several suspects later blew themselves up in an apartment in Leganés, killing a police officer.

### Commuters: routine, vigilance and lingering fear

Passengers interviewed in Madrid in anniversary coverage described a mixture of resilience and unease. Some said they initially avoided the Cercanías system, changed trains or stood near doors after the attacks, but gradually resumed their normal journeys because there was no practical alternative.

Others said the psychological effects remain close to the surface. Sudden stops, emergency announcements or an unattended backpack can produce immediate tension inside a carriage. Survivors and passengers who were traveling that morning have also described particular difficulty returning to the same station or taking a train at the same hour.

Younger commuters and people who moved to Madrid after 2004 tend to experience the network more ordinarily. But for long-term passengers, the station names—especially Atocha and El Pozo—remain inseparable from images of shattered carriages, smoke and commuters helping the injured.

The coping mechanisms commuters most often describe are simple: maintaining routine, avoiding constant discussion of the attack, traveling with friends or relatives when anxiety is high, and treating continued use of public transport as a refusal to be intimidated. A heavier police presence, surveillance cameras and public awareness of suspicious objects have also provided reassurance, although some passengers say visible security can itself recall why it is necessary.

### Fifth-anniversary commemorations

The fifth anniversary was marked with subdued ceremonies rather than large political demonstrations. Victims’ relatives, survivors, railway employees, union representatives and public officials gathered at memorial sites, including **Atocha station**, where flowers and candles were placed and moments of silence observed.

Commemorations also took place at **El Pozo and Santa Eugenia**, and at Madrid’s other memorials to the victims. The best-known is the cylindrical glass monument outside Atocha, containing messages of condolence collected after the bombings; below it is a quiet remembrance chamber inside the station.

Officials and victims’ groups emphasized remembrance and solidarity, though divisions persisted over the political handling and investigation of the attacks. Some families preferred private mourning and criticized anniversary events that became entangled in partisan disputes.

For the thousands passing through Atocha each morning, the anniversary briefly interrupts the normal rhythm of the commute. Trains still arrive crowded, passengers hurry between platforms, and announcements echo through the station. Five years on, Madrid’s principal response is visible in that ordinary movement: the railway remains both a place of mourning and an essential part of daily life.

**MADRID —** More than two decades after bombs ripped through four commuter trains in Madrid, the emotional shock of Spain’s deadliest terrorist attack still surfaces in crowded carriages, station announcements and the annual ringing of bells each March 11.

The 2004 attacks killed 193 people and wounded nearly 2,000 during the morning rush hour. Ten bombs exploded on trains traveling toward the city center, including near Atocha station, transforming an ordinary commute into a scene of shattered railcars, smoke and chaos.

For survivors, victims’ families, emergency workers and witnesses, the passage of time has not erased the trauma. Some continue to struggle with anxiety, depression, insomnia or a heightened fear of public transportation. Others describe grief that returns unexpectedly — with the sound of a train braking, the sight of an abandoned bag or news of violence elsewhere.

The attacks also left a lasting imprint on Madrid itself. Memorials at Atocha station and other locations serve as places of remembrance, while ceremonies each anniversary bring together relatives, public officials and residents. Moments of silence are observed across the capital, and flowers are laid for those killed.

The bombings were carried out by Islamist extremists inspired by al-Qaida, three days before a national election. In the immediate aftermath, confusion and political accusations over who was responsible deepened public anger and mistrust. That turmoil became part of the national memory alongside the loss of life.

Mental health specialists say trauma can persist for years and may re-emerge around anniversaries or after similar events. Recovery does not necessarily mean forgetting, they say, but finding ways to live alongside memories that remain painful.

The attack’s reach extended far beyond those aboard the trains. Police officers, firefighters, medical personnel and ordinary residents rushed to help the injured. Many witnesses carried images from the scene long after the physical debris had been cleared.

Yet the days after the bombings also revealed a powerful civic response. Madrileños stood in lines to donate blood, opened their homes to stranded commuters and joined mass demonstrations against terrorism. That solidarity remains a central part of how the city remembers March 11.

For a new generation, the attacks are increasingly something learned in classrooms or through family stories. For those who experienced them, however, the morning remains sharply personal — a dividing line between life before the explosions and everything that followed.

Madrid’s trains again carry millions of passengers through the capital’s suburbs and center. But each March, the city pauses, and the names of the dead are recalled — a reminder that while the railway was repaired quickly, the emotional wounds have taken far longer to heal.

# Madrid train bombings: Five years later, commuters remember a morning of terror

**By Television News Digital**  
**MADRID, March 11, 2009**

Five years after bombs ripped through packed commuter trains during Madrid’s morning rush hour, regular riders returned Wednesday to the same platforms, rail cars and routes where 191 people were killed and about 1,800 others wounded.

For many, the daily journey through stations such as Atocha, El Pozo and Santa Eugenia has never again felt entirely routine.

Commuters paused at memorials, left flowers and observed moments of silence for the victims of the March 11, 2004, attacks—known across Spain simply as **11-M**. Some riders crossed themselves as they entered Atocha station. Others stood quietly before the glass memorial near the station, where messages written after the bombings preserve the shock and grief that swept the country.

The crowds still arrive every weekday morning, filling the trains from Madrid’s eastern suburbs. But survivors and regular passengers say ordinary sounds—a dropped bag, a sudden bang, an unattended package—can bring back memories of the explosions.

## Ten bombs exploded on four trains

The attack began shortly before 8 a.m. on March 11, 2004, as four commuter trains approached or stopped at stations along the busy rail corridor leading into central Madrid.

Ten bombs hidden in backpacks exploded within minutes of one another at or near Atocha, El Pozo and Santa Eugenia. Three additional devices failed to detonate.

The blasts tore open rail cars crowded with workers, students and other passengers. Seats and windows were blown apart, and personal belongings were scattered along the tracks. Survivors emerged bloodied and disoriented while other passengers, railway employees, police officers and local residents rushed to help.

Emergency crews converted platforms and nearby streets into improvised treatment areas. Buses, taxis and private vehicles carried some of the wounded to hospitals as Madrid’s medical system confronted one of the largest mass-casualty emergencies in modern European history.

The attack killed 191 people and wounded roughly 1,800. Victims came from Spain and numerous other countries, reflecting the immigrant communities that use Madrid’s suburban rail network.

## Investigation turned from ETA to Islamist militants

In the first hours after the bombings, members of Spain’s government publicly focused suspicion on ETA, the armed Basque separatist organization that had carried out decades of attacks.

Investigators soon found evidence pointing in a different direction.

A van linked to the attackers contained detonators and a recording of Quranic verses. A sports bag containing an unexploded bomb gave police critical forensic evidence, including a mobile telephone used as part of the triggering system. Investigators traced the explosives, phones and other materials to a network of Islamist militants and criminal associates.

The bombs had been made with dynamite obtained through contacts connected to a mine in northern Spain. Prosecutors said the group was motivated by extremist ideology associated with al Qaeda, although the court did not find that the plot had been directly ordered by al Qaeda’s central leadership.

The change in the direction of the investigation came just days before Spain’s national election and fueled a fierce political dispute. Critics accused the government of emphasizing ETA because an Islamist attack could be linked in voters’ minds to Spain’s participation in the Iraq war.

On March 14, Socialist leader José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero defeated the governing Popular Party. Zapatero later withdrew Spanish troops from Iraq, as he had promised during the campaign.

## Suspects died in apartment explosion

The search for the bombers accelerated in the weeks after the attacks.

On April 3, 2004, police surrounded an apartment in Leganés, south of Madrid, where several suspects were hiding. As an elite officer entered the building, the men inside detonated explosives, killing themselves and police officer Francisco Javier Torronteras.

Seven suspects died in the blast. Investigators concluded that several of them had played central roles in the train attacks. Their deaths meant that many questions about the planning and leadership of the cell would never be tested fully in court.

## Trial produced convictions and long sentences

The main trial began in February 2007 under heavy security and lasted for months. Twenty-eight defendants faced charges ranging from murder and membership in a terrorist organization to supplying explosives.

In October 2007, Spain’s National Court convicted 21 defendants while acquitting seven. The verdict rejected several conspiracy theories that had alleged ETA involvement or a broader hidden plot.

Three men received the longest sentences:

- **Jamal Zougam**, found guilty of placing bombs on the trains;
- **Othman El Gnaoui**, convicted for his role in the conspiracy and transport of explosives;
- **José Emilio Suárez Trashorras**, a former miner who helped supply the dynamite used in the attacks.

Their nominal sentences totaled tens of thousands of years under Spain’s system of assigning prison terms for each victim and offense. Spanish law, however, limited the amount of time they could actually serve—generally to a maximum of 40 years for the most serious terrorism convictions.

Other defendants were convicted of lesser offenses, including belonging to a terrorist group, collaborating with extremists, trafficking explosives or falsifying documents.

Spain’s Supreme Court later reviewed the case, upholding the central findings while altering some convictions. The appeals process left 18 people convicted in connection with the attacks.

The courts concluded that an Islamist extremist cell carried out the bombings. They did not establish that ETA took part, and they found no proof that the operation was directed by a foreign government or by al Qaeda’s senior command structure.

## A tragedy carried into everyday life

For the commuters who still travel the bombed routes, the legal verdicts did not end the emotional consequences.

Some survivors have continued to receive treatment for burns, hearing loss, damaged limbs and other physical injuries. Many passengers, relatives and emergency workers have also struggled with anxiety, depression, insomnia and post-traumatic stress.

The geography of the attacks makes remembrance unavoidable. Unlike an isolated battlefield or a site closed after a disaster, the railway remains part of Madrid’s daily life. Trains pass the same signals and platforms every few minutes. Passengers sit beside the same kinds of windows and doors shattered in 2004.

At El Pozo and Santa Eugenia, memorials stand near working stations. At Atocha, the translucent memorial bears messages of mourning and solidarity collected after the attack.

Regular riders describe a mixture of persistence and unease. Most have resumed their routines, reading newspapers, listening to music or dozing as the trains move toward the city center. Yet the anniversary brings back images of damaged carriages, sirens and lists of missing passengers.

For relatives of the dead, the morning commute can mark time in a more personal way: the train a loved one boarded, the station where a final telephone call was made, or the route from which that person never returned.

## Spain pauses for 11-M

Anniversary ceremonies have sometimes reflected the political divisions that followed the attacks, including disputes over the government’s initial statements, the Iraq war and competing victims’ associations.

But at the stations, remembrance is often quieter and less political.

Five years later, the rail network again carried hundreds of thousands of passengers through Madrid. Trains arrived, doors opened and commuters hurried toward work and school.

Among the flowers and moments of silence, the central fact of 11-M remained unchanged: an ordinary journey on an ordinary weekday morning became the deadliest terrorist attack in Spain’s history—and for those who ride the same line, the past is never far from the next stop.
